title: Why You Shouldn’t Use A Hand Signal For Quiet Attention iet-attention/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common practice of using a raised-hand signal to call a class to quiet attention, arguing it is insufficient despite good intentions. He identifies three core problems: students must wait for the signal to 'domino' around a noisy room, the visual-only cue is harder to clearly define than words and loses potency once removed from sight, and it simply underperforms what's possible. His recommended alternative is a single, direct verbal cue—'Can I have your attention please?'—which reaches every student simultaneously, carries clear and immediate responsibility, and works from any location. He closes by noting that pairing the verbal cue with well-taught, practiced expectations builds urgency and reliability that outperforms any hand signal.
points: A hand signal for quiet requires waiting for it to visually 'domino' around the room, wasting time especially in noisy settings.
Hand signals are inherently less clear and descriptive than words, and lose potency once the visual cue is out of sight.
Combining a hand signal with verbal reminders and warnings adds confusion rather than clarity.
The recommended alternative is a single verbal cue—'Can I have your attention please?'—that reaches every student simultaneously.
Responsibility to comply begins the instant the verbal cue is spoken, unlike a signal that must be visually noticed first.
quotes: The problem, however, is that even at its best, a hand signal is insufficient for such an important aspect of classroom management.
In other words, unless you already have their attention, a hand signal will take time to domino around the class—especially in a noisy, collaborative learning environment.
The problem with hand signals is that they’re not as clear, as detailed, or as descriptive as a few, simple words can be.

And nothing works better than asking, “Can I have your attention please?” This routine-prompting question communicates precisely what you want, works no matter where you are, and reaches every student at the same time.
It's common for teachers to hold up their quiet signal while at the same time offering reminders, warnings, and admonitions. But this only adds to the confusion.
A single, succinct verbal cue, on the other hand, is a once for all command that stays in play until you say otherwise.
